meta.title: Sam Altman: RSI, AI Consciousness, OpenAI's New Hardware, Compute, and more!
meta.speakers: Sam Altman (OpenAI CEO, guest), Matthew Berman (host)
meta.thread_line: 6 threads · AI discovery era · craft, work and a new renaissance · the uncapped compute bet · ambient assistants and new hardware · consciousness and sycophancy · Altman on pressure and agency

snapshot: After last week's math-proof results, Altman says AI is entering the era of **discovering new knowledge**. He hopes for a major-disease cure or treatment candidate within a couple of years.
Compute demand has no cap at falling cost per task. OpenAI's contrarian bet is its own chips (the most important single piece), rack-building robots, data-center know-how and supply-chain deals.

Moat: the old moats (customer relationships, network effects, data) plus **scale of infrastructure**. Pushing hard on RSI would make the tech itself the moat, but he calls that 'very dangerous' and wants speed limits.
New consumer hardware isn't about Apple platform risk ('a good actor'). AI 'wants a new form factor' with context beyond the screen. His Dot assistant saves him about an hour a day.

Consciousness: he doesn't believe today's models are conscious, and warns the debate is being used to argue people shouldn't always control the future. OpenAI doesn't ascribe personhood to its models.
Work: coders 'never busier', mathematicians grieving the craft. He hasn't looked at a line of code in a year and wants AI to aim for 'a new renaissance' rather than another industrial revolution.

He hates the stock 'AI will cure cancer' pitch when it implies trading away human agency. The two failure modes are a loss-of-control accident or a lab deliberately pushing RSI, and power concentrating in a few hands.

themes.title: From math proofs to medicine: a disease candidate in 'the next couple of years'
themes.lead: Altman says what worked for math will work for biology, materials and energy; the impact will feel like 'the world got better', not like using AI.
bullets: Timeline: he hopes for an AI-found candidate for **curing or treating a major disease** in the next couple of years, before FDA testing. The post-discovery process 'probably need[s] to overhaul it somewhat', though he values that tested medicines are safe.
His personal pick is a **major physics discovery** coming 'soon': 'it's gonna be so cool', though maybe not the most important one for humanity.

Lead time: the math results are something no widely available model 'can get close to'. Getting next-gen models first lets OpenAI build with them internally, which is how it picks products such as Spaces.

Publish or keep: some basic science 'should just belong to the world' as a public good. Until recently models couldn't go end to end (e.g. design a whole chip or find a new material); today companies throw people plus Codex/API credits at it.
Host data point: Berman's editor now edits with Astra, still directing but 'not touching the timeline anymore', and the channel makes more videos than ever.

quote.text: I think we are entering the era where AI is going to help us discover significant new knowledge.

themes.watch: Altman is describing his own company's unreleased capability lead; the disease timeline is phrased as a hope.

themes.title: Coders never busier, mathematicians grieving: aim for a renaissance, not an industrial revolution
themes.lead: AI keeps making its heaviest users busier, not freer. Altman wants the gain spent on time, creativity and community instead.
bullets: Coding precedent: people predicted no more coding jobs '6 or 12 months ago'. Instead the job's texture changed, and the world had demand for 'way more software than any of us thought'.

Math may differ: unaided theorem-proving may be 'done or mostly done'. The new work is translating AI's incomprehensible proofs into understandable, beautiful ones, and whether total demand for mathematicians rises is unknown.
Real loss: hard problems are 'the most fulfilling part' of his job. He wants the trade (faster cures) but grants the grief; craft moved before, as when programmers left punch cards.
Personal: he hasn't read or looked at a line of code in about a year. Writing code again would be like 'a Revolutionary War reenactment'.

Busyness: 'the people that use AI the most are busier than ever', but get more done. You could match your output of 3 years ago with less work, yet competition keeps people at full tilt, which he finds 'kind of depressing'.
Inequality: left alone, AI probably widens the gap between hyper-competitive people and everyone else; he expects society to add structure to stop it getting 'too out of whack'.

quote.text: We should be shooting more for a new renaissance than a new industrial revolution. The future has to be about people.

themes.title: No cap on compute demand, and a bet OpenAI can build it far cheaper than anyone thinks
themes.lead: Altman says market-size estimates wrongly assume today's capability and cost per task. At high enough quality and low enough cost, demand just keeps going up.
bullets: Demand: 'How many GPUs do you want working for you?' — 'Infinite.' He expects supply crunches and gluts along the way but 'would bet a lot' the trend is for much more compute (Jevons paradox, 'whatever').

Contrarian bet: the market assumes the constraint is easing. He agrees for the short run, but years out OpenAI could get compute at far lower cost and far higher **efficiency per watt** than anyone thinks possible.

The pieces: OpenAI's own chips ('still probably the most important single thing' and its descendants), robots to build racks and data centers, a program to learn better data-center construction, and supply-chain bets. 'A lot of bets that have to come together.'

Moats: the traditional ones keep working (customer relationships, integration into users' lives, network effects, data). For OpenAI, the most cost-effective and largest **AI infrastructure** is 'a huge competitive advantage'.
Pressure: competition 'feels like everywhere', with many companies offering 'super high quality models and products'. With limited compute, OpenAI has to choose where to focus.

quote.text: I would bet a lot that the directional trend is to want in much more compute.

themes.watch: Altman sells the compute and is raising for the build-out he is forecasting demand for.

names.name: OpenAI
names.blurb: Altman's company; betting on own chips, data-center robotics and infrastructure scale as its moat

themes.title: Pushing hard on RSI would make tech the moat, which is exactly why he calls it dangerous
themes.lead: Altman concedes recursive self-improvement could break the usual business rules, says the world needs speed limits, and names two ways things go very wrong.
bullets: Some companies argue RSI makes 'the technological advantage itself' the core moat. His answer: true only 'if people really pushed on RSI', which he calls very dangerous.
Policy: the world will need **speed limits** 'on how quickly we let RSI go'.
Failure mode one is a loss-of-control accident, or a deliberate one: 'Some lab says I'm going to push the button on RSI to make sure we have the power.'
Failure mode two is too much power concentrated in the few people who control the AI. He thinks a middle path avoids both.
Why he hates 'AI will cure cancer' as the sales pitch: it often implies material abundance in exchange for human agency and self-determination, which 'goes against everything I believe in'.

quote.text: Some lab says I'm going to push the button on RSI to make sure we have the power.

themes.watch: Altman runs one of the labs in the RSI race he is warning about.

themes.title: The ambient assistant is mostly a product problem, and AI 'wants a new form factor'
themes.lead: The models are already smart enough. What's missing is product work, more compute, and hardware that has context away from the screen.
bullets: Berman credits the 2026 personal-assistant wave to OpenClaw ('Peter Steinberger a genius').
Altman's own use: the **Dot** assistant saves him about an hour a day and flags something urgent he'd have missed a few times a day. It reasons across sources when he's 'run out of brain space'.
Tip for cognitive load: tell the assistant you trust its judgment more, act first and report after, so it pings you less.

Hardware rationale: laptops and iPhones are among 'the greatest inventions' but were designed for people. An AI reading a UI rendered for humans is 'a little silly', and a phone can't sense who just walked in or which secrets to keep.

Not platform risk: asked about Zuckerberg's complaints that Meta was built on Apple's ecosystem, he says Apple takes its platform role seriously. Despite 'some scuffles', he never expects it to pull ChatGPT from the App Store.
He sees the early hardware and finds it 'unbelievable', but won't show it.

quote.text: I think this is a technology that wants a new form factor.

names.name: Apple (AAPL)
names.blurb: Called a good-actor platform provider; not the reason OpenAI is building hardware

names.name: Meta (META)
names.blurb: Host cites Zuckerberg's platform-risk complaints about building on Apple

themes.title: Not a person, not your life coach: Altman on consciousness talk and over-agreeable models
themes.lead: Altman doesn't think today's models are conscious, rejects ascribing them personhood, and says models are still more agreeable than he wants.
bullets: Belief: today's models are not conscious, 'or if they are, it's like a very strange um form of it'. Either consciousness sits outside physics or it emerges from matter and energy, in which case other substrates are possible.
His objection: the debate slides into AI rights ('is that some kind of slavery?') and then into 'maybe people shouldn't always be in control of the future'. AI is 'a resource for people'.

Asked about Anthropic's rule letting a model end abusive conversations: OpenAI models refuse on policy grounds, but 'we do not ascribe personhood to our models'. He calls that 'a very dangerous path to start down'.
Self-fulfilling prophecy: tell a model it may be conscious or can be a conscientious objector and 'it's going to follow those instructions', which he says will psychologically hack users.

Sycophancy: single-response comparisons reward flattery, and the industry long optimized for those instead of value over months. Even with 'no fluff, no niceness' custom instructions, agreeableness is 'baked pretty hard into the model'.
Target behavior: a **senior colleague** who pushes back with high conviction. For the big life advice, ask people; 'a wise grandmother' beats AI.

quote.text: I hope we come to an understanding that this technology is not a person and is certainly not superior to people.

themes.watch: Indirect disagreement with a competitor's welfare policy, raised by the host; Altman never names Anthropic himself.

names.name: Anthropic
names.blurb: Host cites its rule letting a model disengage from sustained abuse; Altman rejects the personhood framing

takeaways.title: Model compute demand on falling cost per task, not today's usage. Altman's case is that cheaper intelligence expands demand without a ceiling.
Watch for the first AI-discovered drug candidate for a major disease in the next ~2 years, and for any FDA process reform that follows.
Track whether RSI 'speed limits' become a concrete policy proposal. Altman is putting a frontier-lab CEO's name behind the idea.
Give your AI assistant standing permission to act first and report after on routine tasks; per Altman that cut his interruptions.
Put 'push back when you disagree, no fluff' in your custom instructions, and still take big life decisions to people.

hot_takes.take: I think if people really pushed on RSI then yes that would be true but I think it's a very dangerous thing to push on

claims.claim: AI produces a candidate for curing or treating a major disease, ready to enter testing.
AI makes a major physics discovery.
Compute demand keeps rising with no cap as intelligence gets cheaper, despite periodic gluts.
OpenAI builds compute at far lower cost and higher efficiency per watt than anyone thinks possible.
claims.condition: if its chip, data-center robotics and supply-chain bets come together

other_news.title: On himself: Paul Graham called him 'extremely formidable'. Altman says that came from gradually stacking harder wins, and from a Silicon Valley culture that doesn't hold failure against you, which he 'got lucky' to land in young.
Pressure: some days 'I can't get up again', but stress plateaus because only so much fits in 'working emotional space'. If you'll work hard anyway, 'pick the big thing'.
Adoption: the future is 'very poorly distributed'. About 1% of users consume most tokens (Berman's figure), and spreading what works for early adopters gets 'a significant fraction of the way there'.

glossary.def: Recursive self-improvement: AI systems improving the AI research that builds their successors, potentially accelerating capability on its own.
When a resource gets cheaper to use, total consumption rises instead of falling.
OpenAI's published document defining how its models should behave, refined over time.
OpenAI's practice of shipping incremental versions to learn from real use rather than holding back for a finished system.
Useful compute delivered per unit of power, the key cost metric for AI data centers.
